query: Reading the Floor {Every famous bout in the Duelling Hall left its mark on the floor, a scorch or a frost-crack or a gouge. Old duellists say you can read a fight in the boards.|The floor again. You've learned which scorch belongs to which year's champion, from the plaques on the wall.|You can read the boards now, more or less: here someone parried late; here someone lost their nerve and their eyebrows.} {Today a fresh burn sits on top of the old ones.|The cleaners have been, and the boards shine like a map under glass.|{season == "winter": The hall is freezing and the boards creak under every step.|Dust hangs in the long light from the windows.}} Trace an old bout through {You follow a duel from the first scorch to the final frost-crack, step by step, until you know where the loser went wrong. Your knees ache from crawling.|You walk a champion's footwork across the burns, slowly, like learning a dance from its footprints. It's tiring, careful work.|You read a whole tournament final in the floor and find the moment it turned, a single mark the size of a coin. You stand up stiff and certain.} Scrub the floor for the club {The club pays a crown or two for scrubbing. You scrub until the boards gleam and your arms burn.|You scrub, and the old marks stay, as they always do; the dirt goes. You're paid in coins and a sore back.|You know which boards to go easy on: the famous ones. The club treasurer pays you, and adds a nod.}
